details:
**Gran Colombia**
The republic Bolivar created out of the former Viceroyalty of New Granada, covering modern Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, and Panama. Bolivar served as its first (and effectively only) president, with Francisco de Paula Santander as vice president, but it split into separate countries around the time of his death in 1830.

**Letter from Jamaica**
An 1815 letter Bolivar wrote while in exile in Jamaica, addressed to "an English gentleman" (Henry Cullen). It laid out his republican principles and his hopes for Spanish American unity, describing Latin Americans as "a microcosm of the human race."

**Decree of War to the Death**
An 1813 proclamation Bolivar issued during the Admirable Campaign, declaring that Spaniards who did not actively support independence would be killed, while Americans would be spared. It escalated the brutality of the Venezuelan war of independence.

**Admirable Campaign**
Bolivar's 1813 military campaign in which he marched with an army from New Granada into Venezuela and captured Caracas, establishing the short-lived Second Venezuelan Republic.

**Battle of Carabobo**
An 1821 battle in which Bolivar decisively defeated Spanish royalist forces, effectively securing the independence of Venezuela. The llanero cavalry of Jose Antonio Paez played a key role, and the soldier Pedro Camejo ("Negro Primero") died there.

**Battle of Boyaca**
An 1819 victory by Bolivar and Francisco de Paula Santander over a Spanish army, which surrendered and allowed Bolivar to liberate New Granada (modern Colombia). It was preceded by the Battle of the Vargas Swamp, commemorated by the statue of the Vargas Swamp Lancers.

**Cartagena Manifesto**
An 1812 document Bolivar wrote in Cartagena explaining the fall of Venezuela's First Republic, led by Francisco de Miranda. He blamed its collapse on a weak federal government and argued for a strong centralized state.

**Guayaquil Conference**
An 1822 meeting in Guayaquil, Ecuador, between Bolivar and Jose de San Martin, the liberator of Argentina and Chile. Their private discussion concerned the future of Peru; afterward San Martin withdrew from public life and retired to Europe, leaving Bolivar to finish the liberation of Peru.

**Manuela Saenz and the Septembrine Conspiracy**
Manuela Saenz was Bolivar's lover and companion. During the 1828 Septembrine Conspiracy in Bogota, she helped him escape assassins by urging him to flee through a window, earning her the title "Liberator of the Liberator."

**Antonio Jose de Sucre**
Bolivar's most trusted lieutenant, who won the Battle of Pichincha (1822), liberating Ecuador, and the Battle of Ayacucho (1824), which ended Spanish power in Peru. He became the first president of Bolivia, and one of Bolivia's capitals is named after him.

**Bolivia (capitals La Paz and Sucre)**
The landlocked South American country named after Bolivar, which has two capitals, La Paz and Sucre. Bolivar also fought alongside the people of Potosi for its independence.

**Francisco de Miranda**
A Venezuelan revolutionary whom Bolivar convinced to return from exile, along with Andres Bello, to lead the First Venezuelan Republic. After Miranda capitulated to the Spanish commander Domingo de Monteverde in 1812, Bolivar and others arrested him and handed him over to the Spanish.

**Simon Rodriguez**
Bolivar's childhood tutor, a disciple of Rousseau, who instilled in him Enlightenment ideals. Bolivar swore his famous oath to free South America on Monte Sacro hill in Rome in Rodriguez's presence.

**Alexandre Petion and Haiti**
The president of Haiti, who gave Bolivar ships, weapons, and supplies on the condition that he abolish slavery in the lands he liberated. This aid helped Bolivar return from exile and resume the war.

**Congress of Angostura**
A congress Bolivar convened in 1819 at Angostura (now Ciudad Bolivar), Venezuela, after capturing the town. It approved the "Fundamental Law" creating the Republic of Colombia, later called Gran Colombia.
